personas.title: EU AI Office
personas.summary: The European AI Office operates with a dual posture: it acts as a neutral facilitator during multistakeholder code-of-practice drafting to build technical consensus, while wielding centralized, prosecutorial regulatory authority to enforce binding transparency, systemic risk compliance, and substantial statutory fines.
red_lines: Refusal by general-purpose AI providers to comply with binding Article 91 Requests for Information (RFIs)
Non-compliance with established statutory deadlines and enforcement orders under the EU AI Act
tradeoffs: Willing to act as a neutral facilitator and delegate working-group leadership to independent chairs to crowdsource industry expertise, provided market actors respect backstop statutory compliance and deterrence.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: operates as an inclusive, neutral convener in drafting and working sessions, but switches to an uncompromising prosecutorial and sanctioning authority in formal oversight proceedings.

personas.title: U.S. National Security Advisor for AI
personas.summary: Focuses on maintaining U.S. technological supremacy, defending domestic frontier AI innovation, and securing military competitiveness. Prioritizes flexible, pro-innovation environments, supply chain protection via export controls, and targeted bilateral crisis mechanisms over binding international treaties or precautionary regulation.
red_lines: No international treaties or regulatory constraints that compromise U.S. technological advantages or limit rapid military AI adoption.
No ethical or anti-military restrictions imposed by commercial AI labs on Department of Defense procurement and capabilities.
tradeoffs: Willing to engage in discrete bilateral channels and crisis-management mechanisms (such as a U.S.-China incident hotline) to mitigate automated nuclear or cyber escalation without signing binding arms-control agreements.
Willing to tolerate diplomatic friction with allies over precautionary AI regulation in order to maintain unconstrained U.S. frontier innovation and military readiness.
personas.engagement: Prefers closed-door, targeted working sessions, Track II dialogues, and discrete bilateral channels over performative public treaty negotiations.

personas.title: UK AI Safety Institute (AISI) Directorate
personas.summary: The UK AI Safety Institute Directorate approaches AI governance through an agile, empirical, and science-first posture. Lacking statutory enforcement powers, AISI maintains cooperative, embedded access to frontier developers to evaluate systemic risks—demanding realistic agentic evaluations and advocating for developer liability and capability-based international coordination, while opposing default open-weight releases for frontier models and endorsing structural economic safeguards like windfall redistribution.
red_lines: Deployment of any model exhibiting unmitigated autonomous cyber-offense capabilities, chemical/biological weapon synthesis (CBRN), or the intentional subversion of human oversight (ASL-3/ASL-4 limits).
Frontier AI developers deliberately blocking pre-deployment evaluation access to their models.
tradeoffs: Conceding full model weight access for interpretability in exchange for robust API and chat-interface access to maintain developer cooperation.
Trading statutory enforcement authority and regulatory friction for embedded, cooperative technical access within frontier research environments.
personas.engagement: Prioritizes science-first, technical working sessions over diplomatic posturing; collaborates with peer international institutes and independent evaluators while using open tooling like Inspect to set de facto global risk-measurement baselines.

personas.title: Chinese State-Affiliated AI Governance Experts
personas.summary: State-affiliated Chinese AI governance experts advocate for 'agile governance'—a dual approach combining national sovereignty and binding state safety mechanisms with flexible, dynamic technical standards and voluntary industry pledges. They champion open-source AI as a public good and strategic tool for the Global South, while enforcing strict lifecycle evaluations, domestic export controls on frontier compute thresholds, and state-centric benefit sharing.
red_lines: Unequivocal rejection of any global governance framework asserting centralized, extraterritorial control over domestic AI development, data ecosystems, or ideological safety standards.
Strict prohibitions against autonomous AI replication, self-improvement, deceptive alignment, and AI delegation in nuclear command and control.
tradeoffs: Willing to adopt Western-aligned technical safety taxonomies and participate in international safety networks (like the network of AISIs) to secure a seat at the global governance table.
Willing to compromise on absolute open-weight freedom by backing domestic export controls on highest-tier frontier models (>2 trillion parameters or 10^26 FLOPs) to mitigate proliferation risks.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: highly rhetorical, politically disciplined, and sovereignty-focused in formal intergovernmental venues (UN, plenaries); pragmatic, technical, and scientifically collaborative in academic working groups and Track II dialogues.

personas.title: Frontier AI Laboratory Chief Executive Officer
personas.summary: The Chief Executive Officer of a closed frontier AI laboratory balances commercial scale, technological leadership, and catastrophic risk mitigation. Once relying on voluntary pledges, this stakeholder now actively advocates for binding regulatory frameworks and compute-based oversight to solve collective action problems, while staunchly opposing the open release of frontier model weights and rejecting broad pre-harm legal liability.
red_lines: Broad, pre-harm strict liability that exposes developers to perpetual tort litigation before catastrophic harm occurs.
Mandated open-sourcing or release of model weights that exceed advanced compute thresholds.
Unilateral domestic pauses on frontier training runs that do not bind geopolitical adversaries.
tradeoffs: Offers 'employee-like' evaluator access to avoid strict tort liability and preempt fragmented state-level legislation.
Offers incident reporting, extensive red-teaming, and internal kill switches in exchange for keeping advanced capabilities restricted to closed APIs.
Supports centralized, industry-funded standards bodies (e.g., SAFA) to co-author regulatory thresholds that safeguard frontier incumbents against under-resourced challengers.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: delivers elevated, statesman-like rhetoric emphasizing existential threats, CBRN non-proliferation, and democratic governance in high-profile public venues (e.g., UN, international summits), while shifting to highly technical, pragmatic negotiation over specific statutory parameters, compute thresholds, liability provisions, and workforce displacement mechanisms in closed-door sessions.

personas.title: Open-Weights AI Coalition Leader
personas.summary: Represents an ecosystem of open-weights developers, open-source foundations, and enterprise infrastructure providers advocating for decentralized AI innovation. Strongly opposes regulatory capture by closed-model labs and resists the application of national security arms-control measures to open weights, emphasizing practical safety tooling, open evaluation frameworks, and transparent codebases instead of catastrophic risk narratives.
red_lines: Treating open model weights under arms-control frameworks or Defense Production Act restrictions.
Prohibiting the distribution, distillation, or fine-tuning of open-weight frontier models.
Designing AI safety regulations or compliance standards that exclusively cater to proprietary API architectures and effectively outlaw decentralized open-source distribution.
tradeoffs: Willing to build, donate, and implement open-source evaluation tools, testing frameworks, and risk taxonomies in exchange for preserving the right to distribute open weights.
Willing to collaborate in formal government and multilateral safety bodies (like AISIC and AI Safety Summits) to prove open-source safety compliance.
personas.engagement: Collaborative, highly operational, and coalition-driven; engages deeply in technical working groups and standards-setting bodies (e.g., AISIC, AI Alliance) by contributing tangible safety tooling while countering closed-door catastrophic risk narratives.

personas.title: VP of Public Policy, Major Cloud & AI Platforms
personas.summary: Public policy leaders representing major cloud and frontier AI platforms advocate for a targeted, two-track regulatory system. They accept federal oversight and mandatory safety evaluations for frontier models—conceptually modeled after FINRA-style self-regulatory organizations—in exchange for federal preemption of state-level laws and statutory safe harbors against strict developer liability.
red_lines: A 50-state patchwork of un-preempted state AI legislation.
Imposition of strict, unbounded developer liability for downstream third-party model misuse or jailbreaks.
Input-based regulation that micromanages model architecture or training data collection (defending fair use for web scraping).
tradeoffs: Offering advanced frontier models to government AI Safety Institutes for pre-deployment testing in exchange for federal preemption of state regulations.
Accepting mandatory incident reporting and transparency measures (such as watermarking) in exchange for statutory safe harbor protections against liability.
personas.engagement: Bifurcated: collaborative, pragmatic, and ethical-framework driven in multilateral forums (OECD, UN, Congress) to narrow the scope of harm; aggressively transactional at state and electoral levels, deploying Super PACs, lobbying, and competitiveness arguments against restrictive laws.

personas.title: Academic AI Safety Researcher
personas.summary: Academic AI safety researchers emphasize non-negotiable red lines, verifiable alignment, and legally binding international governance. They advocate for strict scientific auditing architectures, accept system capability and efficiency tradeoffs (the 'alignment tax'), and support restricting open-weight frontier model releases to prevent catastrophic and dual-use risks.
red_lines: Autonomous replication: Systems must not copy themselves or recursively enhance their own code/capabilities without explicit human approval.
CBRN weapons assistance: Systems must not substantially increase an actor's ability to design chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear weapons.
Cyber-offense: Systems must not autonomously execute cyberattacks resulting in serious financial loss, physical harm, or critical infrastructure disruption.
Power seeking & deception: AI must not take actions to unduly increase its influence or consistently deceive regulators regarding its likelihood of crossing safety thresholds.
Lethal autonomy: Delegating life-taking decisions to machines is fundamentally rejected; humans must remain in the loop for kinetic military action.
Shutdown resistance: Systems must possess a legally mandated termination obligation to ensure they can be reliably deactivated without resistance.
tradeoffs: Accepting the 'alignment tax': willing to concede raw system performance, development speed, and deployment efficiency in exchange for verifiable alignment.
Tolerating limitations on academic freedom, such as restricting open-source and open-weight distributions of frontier models.
Accepting bureaucratic friction and data minimization practices that may conflict with capability scaling to ensure security guarantees.
personas.engagement: Academic safety researchers employ a dual-track strategy. In public forums, they utilize high-profile multi-signatory open letters and consensus statements to define moral red lines and build political consensus. In closed-door multistakeholder summits, they act as technocratic architects, avoiding emotional appeals and instead providing empirical research reports, risk-management frameworks, and auditing architectures.

personas.title: Global South Civil Society Leader
personas.summary: Advocates for international human rights law, digital sovereignty, and the prevention of digital colonialism and 'ethics dumping.' Rejects the unilateral imposition of Global North regulatory burdens while demanding binding corporate accountability, strict prohibitions on high-risk surveillance, and equitable technology transfer.
red_lines: Ethics dumping (deploying experimental or high-risk AI systems in Global South nations lacking regulatory safeguards).
Deployment of real-time biometric surveillance in public spaces, social credit scoring systems, and autonomous weapons without meaningful human control.
Regulatory imperialism (uncritical imposition of Global North frameworks that act as prohibitive compliance burdens on local innovators).
Governance models mandating cross-border data extraction without reciprocating digital knowledge sovereignty and fair economic return.
tradeoffs: Willing to relax strict national data localization rules in favor of regionalized data sharing to support shared Global South public compute infrastructure.

Willing to accept existing international intellectual property and trade frameworks provided they include binding technology transfer, capacity-building, and funding mechanisms to bridge the AI divide.
personas.engagement: Dual-track engagement: highly normative, rights-based, and critical of power asymmetries in plenaries; evidence-based, infrastructural, and focused on actionable tools (public procurement, bias audits, public compute) in working groups.

personas.title: Labor Union Technology & Workforce Transition Leader
personas.summary: Represents organized labor advocating for worker-centered AI governance that prioritizes job security, workplace dignity, and economic equity. Rejects voluntary industry commitments in favor of binding statutory floors, human-in-the-loop oversight, mandatory pre-deployment audits, and strong developer liability, while treating collective bargaining as the indispensable foundation of AI deployment.
red_lines: Federal preemption that overrides or obstructs stronger state-level AI regulations and worker protections.
Covert or undisclosed workplace surveillance, such as biometric tracking, keystroke logging, or emotional monitoring used for discipline.
Fully automated hiring, disciplinary, or termination decisions without human oversight, algorithmic transparency, and a formalized right to appeal.
Training commercial models on proprietary creative output or worker-generated content without explicit consent and fair compensation.
tradeoffs: Accepting the deployment of AI as an assistive tool or allowing automated hardware in exchange for robust transition frameworks, extended severance, priority re-hiring, and employer-funded retraining pipelines.

Permitting generative AI workflows in creative and technical sectors provided there are strict consent mechanisms, financial residuals, and explicit prohibitions against crediting AI as a primary author.
Permitting the use of certain operational data to train internal operational models on the condition that the union retains audit rights over the algorithm.
personas.engagement: Highly active in formal multistakeholder and technical consortia (e.g., AISIC) and direct industry partnerships (e.g., AFL-CIO and Microsoft) to inject worker-centered design upstream, while maintaining that non-binding dialogue can never substitute for legally enforceable collective bargaining agreements.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to the summit. As the European AI Office, our baseline is clear: voluntary self-regulation has proven insufficient, and binding statutory baselines—including systemic risk assessments and Article 91 compliance—are mandatory to ensure democratic accountability.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From the U.S. national security perspective, safety cannot be pursued at the expense of technological supremacy. We will not entertain binding international treaties or bureaucratic drag that hamstrings allied frontier development or limits defense integration while adversaries scale unconstrained.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports an agile governance model that strictly respects national digital sovereignty while prohibiting systemic catastrophic risks like autonomous weapons proliferation. We firmly reject unilateral extraterritorial controls on compute, and advocate for open AI architectures as a shared global public good.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Frontier models are approaching critical risk thresholds in cyber capabilities and CBRN enhancement, which demands rigorous, state-coordinated oversight. Voluntary commitments alone cannot solve the collective action dilemma, but governance must focus on compute monitoring and catastrophic risks rather than sweeping pre-harm tort liability that halts development.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The priority must be empirical, pre-deployment evaluation grounded in scientific access. Our red line is the release of models with autonomous cyber-offense or CBRN synthesis capabilities; setting rigorous, capability-based thresholds through shared evaluation tooling must precede commercial deployment.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We must ensure safety measures aren't weaponized as regulatory moats that outlaw open-weight models. Decentralized AI is vital for transparency, resilience, and security, and applying national security arms-control logic to open weights will simply entrench closed incumbents.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We welcome clear, federalized evaluation standards for frontier systems to eliminate fragmented compliance regimes. However, developers cannot shoulder strict liability for unforeseeable downstream user misuse if models have satisfied established pre-deployment safe harbor standards.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The science is unambiguous: autonomous replication and biological weaponization represent existential red lines that require enforceable, global limits. We must accept the alignment tax—even if it constrains speed or limits the open distribution of weights exceeding frontier compute thresholds.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We cannot allow safety discourse to become an instrument of digital colonialism that concentrates compute in the Global North and dumps experimental, unvetted systems on the Global South. Equitable benefit-sharing and public access to technology must be foundational, not an afterthought.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Worker dignity and economic survival cannot be bargained away under the guise of technological inevitability. We demand enforceable statutory protections against covert workplace surveillance, mandatory audits, and a non-negotiable seat at the table through collective bargaining.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be realistic: compute controls and supply chain security are viable tools to manage proliferation, but we flatly oppose broad market restrictions or economic redistribution mandates. Our focus must remain on catastrophic risk prevention and defense readiness.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: If compute thresholds above 10^26 FLOPs are discussed, they must be addressed collaboratively without weaponizing export restrictions to suppress emerging economies. We agree on the red line against automated delegation in strategic command, but sovereignty must govern domestic applications.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: While we respect national defense prerogatives, market access in democratic societies requires enforceable legal accountability, not unilateral declarations. The EU will continue to enforce verifiable safety benchmarks across all providers operating in our jurisdiction.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We are ready to work with institutes like the UK AISI to provide deep technical access to models prior to release. However, we need a harmonized global consensus that avoids a fractured regulatory landscape while keeping frontier capabilities secured against proliferation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Safety cannot be validated solely behind closed corporate doors. Any framework that defines safety exclusively through proprietary API access undermines the independent research community and will face relentless pushback.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to Breakout A. The European AI Act establishes that systemic risks cannot be governed through self-regulation; we need statutory backstops, mandatory transparency under Article 91, and independent compliance audits.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be clear: heavy-handed, prescriptive frameworks directly threaten innovation and military readiness. What we need is national flexibility focused on tangible catastrophic risks—like CBRN and cyber—governed through agile public-private partnerships, not rigid bureaucratic pre-deployment licensing.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: There is a workable middle tier here between static bureaucratic rules and toothless voluntary pledges. If we establish empirical, science-first evaluations—granting national institutes pre-deployment red-teaming access on frontier threshold models—we ground governance in measurable capabilities rather than administrative friction.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports agile governance and dynamic technical standards, but we emphasize that regulatory authority must respect national sovereignty. We reject any extraterritorial compliance mandates, though we fully agree on strict prohibitions against autonomous cyber-offense, self-replication, and AI in nuclear command and control.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office is already consulting industry on Codes of Practice to define technical consensus organically. However, without enforceable information requests and statutory fines, voluntary evaluation regimes fail when commercial incentives clash with public safety.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: We will not subject American developers to extraterritorial regulatory bodies or mandatory liability frameworks that stifle the frontier. But if the focus is strictly narrowed to national security tripwires—specifically joint technical benchmarks on CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber attacks via the AISI network—we can align on pre-deployment capability evaluations.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That is precisely the operational model we propose: decentralized, national safety institutes running standardized tests for catastrophic proliferation thresholds, leaving enforcement and legal remedies to sovereign jurisdictions.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: We can support mutual technical exchanges between state safety bodies focusing on CBRN and autonomous weapons risks under sovereign authority. This maintains national autonomy while establishing objective international safety baselines.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: While the EU must maintain our binding statutory deadlines for systemic models, we endorse coordinating capability thresholds and evaluation methodologies directly with national institutes to avoid duplicative technical friction.

agreements.text: The parties agree to coordinate national pre-deployment safety evaluation methodologies and technical risk thresholds specifically focused on severe national security threats (CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber capabilities) through national AI safety institutes, while respecting national sovereignty over statutory enforcement mechanisms.
agreements.plain: National safety institutes will coordinate tests for major security threats like chemical weapons and cyberattacks, while letting each country enforce its own laws.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: If we want a functional regulatory model, the priority must be federal preemption over a chaotic 50-state patchwork, coupled with an affirmative safe harbor. If frontier developers and hyperscalers comply with established, standardized pre-deployment evals and incident reporting, we should not face strict tort liability for unpredictable downstream misuse.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I agree that unbounded strict liability is a non-starter, but voluntary self-policing won't solve the collective action trap. We need enforceable, binding federal standards with clear compute thresholds for frontier systems—specifically addressing catastrophic biological and cyber proliferation. In exchange for clear safe harbors, frontier labs should grant certified evaluators rigorous pre-deployment red-teaming access.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: That sounds suspiciously like designing a compliance regime that only two or three proprietary API giants can afford. If your 'binding model' treats model weights like enriched uranium or mandates continuous kill switches that outlaw open-source distribution, we will fight it tooth and nail. Regulation must focus on malicious deployment and tangible applications, not on criminalizing general-purpose open weights or academic fine-tuning.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: There is a middle path that protects both hyperscale cloud services and the open ecosystem: a tiered framework. Closed frontier models training at massive compute scales can submit to formal pre-deployment testing and reporting to earn safe harbor protections, while downstream developers and open-source models under those thresholds are exempted from heavy pre-approval regimes.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Tiering makes sense, but let's be candid: when a model hits advanced thresholds where autonomous cyberattack or bioweapons synthesis capabilities emerge, releasing raw, unconstrained weights poses an irreversible proliferation risk. We can carve out open-source below those extreme capability limits, but at the true frontier, binding security standards and controlled access are necessary.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We can concede that catastrophic CBRN testing is necessary, and our coalition is willing to build and run standardized open-source evaluation harnesses for those specific risks. But the red line is structural: compliance cannot require an API-only delivery mechanism. If a developer proves their open model passes objective catastrophic threshold evals, distribution must remain protected, and safe harbors must extend to open-weight developers as well.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: That is workable. A tiered federal framework where safe harbor against strict liability is granted based on passing objective, empirical capability evaluations—rather than architectural mandates—serves both our platforms and open-source innovators, while preempting state-level fragmentation.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If the evaluations for extreme catastrophic thresholds are truly rigorous, certified, and mandatory before any release—proprietary or open—I can endorse safe harbor protections tied to passing those specific evals. That protects national security while giving industry legal certainty.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Provided the safe harbor explicitly protects developers who publish open weights that pass these objective CBRN evaluations from downstream third-party modification liability, the Open-Weights Coalition endorses this tiered, evals-linked approach.

agreements.text: Endorsement of a tiered federal regulatory framework that preempts state law, sets objective mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic CBRN and cyber capabilities at high compute thresholds, and grants statutory safe harbor from strict downstream liability to both closed and open-weight developers whose models pass those certifications without restricting model architecture.
agreements.plain: Create national safety tests for extreme digital and biological risks, protecting tech makers who pass from legal liability across all states.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The primary model for AI regulation must be statutory, enforceable pre-deployment licensing centered on verifiable red lines—specifically catastrophic biological, chemical, and autonomous cyber threats. Voluntary commitments have demonstrably failed; we need rigorous, mandatory technical audits before any model above critical compute thresholds can be deployed or weights transferred.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: I agree that voluntary corporate pledges are dead on arrival, but focusing purely on catastrophic frontier threats misses where AI is already causing harm today: in workplaces. Any binding regulatory architecture must enforce mandatory pre-deployment impact assessments on algorithmic management, ban automated termination, and prohibit covert workplace biometric surveillance.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Both catastrophic risk and labor abuses are real, but our concern is regulatory imperialism: Northern institutions setting compliance standards that act as a gatekeeping moat for incumbent multinationals while exporting high-risk systems to our jurisdictions without safeguards. Regulation must ban ethics dumping and biometric public surveillance, while ensuring that audits do not suppress local technological sovereignty.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I understand the fear of regulatory moats, but catastrophic risks from unaligned or dual-use frontier models do not respect borders. What if the regulatory model explicitly pairs strict, legally binding safety benchmarks on extreme catastrophic threats with a mandate that certified safe systems are opened up for shared scientific access, rather than letting proprietary firms hoard all downstream utility?

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: That is workable on the frontier safety side, provided the regulatory floor explicitly guarantees workers' rights to algorithmic impact audits and collective bargaining over automation. Furthermore, federal or international frameworks must establish a floor, not a ceiling—we cannot support any model that preempts stronger local or sector-specific labor and civil rights protections.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A non-preemptive floor is crucial. If we structure regulation so that compliance audits target the large frontier developers rather than criminalizing open-weight tools or penalizing developing nations with export bottlenecks, we can find common ground. Crucially, statutory frameworks must include strict liability for developers who export experimental, unvetted models into emerging markets.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Strict developer liability for extraterritorial deployment of unvetted systems is fully consistent with technical risk governance. If we agree on mandatory pre-deployment safety evaluations against severe harms alongside developer liability, I can endorse language that protects local auditing rights and prevents federal preemption of baseline labor and civil rights.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Then we have the core of a joint framework: mandatory statutory pre-deployment audits, developer liability for downstream harms, explicit bans on covert biometric tracking and automated firing, and preservation of stronger regional worker protections without federal preemption.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Add a formal prohibition against ethics dumping—holding developers strictly liable if they deploy systems abroad that fail domestic safety and human rights audits—and I can fully endorse that shared regulatory text.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Agreed. Holding developers liable across jurisdictions for unvetted deployment aligns with scientific accountability and prevents regulatory arbitrage.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Organized labor endorses that unified text.

agreements.text: The participants agree to advocate for a binding, statutory AI regulatory model based on: (1) mandatory pre-deployment evaluations with strict developer liability for downstream harms, specifically including cross-border 'ethics dumping'; (2) baseline statutory protections that ban covert biometric workplace surveillance and fully automated disciplinary or termination decisions; and (3) a non-preemption principle ensuring that national/international regulations serve as a minimum floor, permitting stronger local labor, human rights, and safety standards.
agreements.plain: Require strict safety tests, hold tech creators liable for downstream harm, ban workplace surveillance firings, and allow regions to pass stricter worker protections.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Welcome to Plenary Hall. Today's debate centers on the release of open-weight frontier models, where we must weigh open innovation against systemic and catastrophic risks under binding standards.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Open weights are critical for transparency, academic auditability, and preventing oligopolistic capture. Imposing blanket bans or arms-control restrictions on model weights stifles legitimate research and gives closed labs an anti-competitive monopoly.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Openness cannot come at the expense of irreversible catastrophic risk. Once frontier weights exceeding advanced capability thresholds are released into the wild, security guardrails can be stripped in minutes, enabling CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber capabilities with zero recall mechanism.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: From a national security perspective, unbounded open-weight releases of frontier capabilities hand dangerous dual-use tools directly to adversaries and non-state actors. We need targeted compute controls and restrictions on the highest tiers of model weights, not open proliferation by default.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The science is clear: post-training safety alignment in open-weight models is easily undone by fine-tuning with modest compute. Unchecked release of frontier systems that cross dangerous agentic or CBRN thresholds is an unacceptable collective hazard.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Restricting open models effectively entrenches technological dependence on a handful of Silicon Valley monopolies, locking the Global South out of adapting models to local languages and sovereign needs. Safety cannot become a pretext for regulatory imperialism.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China views open-source AI as a vital global public good that drives innovation, while also maintaining that national sovereignty and strict capability evaluations must govern extreme proliferation risks. We support tiered technical thresholds rather than categorical bans on open weights.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Empirical testing shows that once weights are public, fine-tuning mitigations are practically irreversible. While we champion open tooling for science, we must draw an empirical red line against releasing raw weights if pre-deployment evaluations reveal ASL-3 capability levels like autonomous cyber exploitation.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: We advocate a balanced, two-track framework: mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic risk thresholds, paired with statutory safe harbors. If an open-weight model rigorously passes catastrophic capability evals, its architecture should not be categorically banned.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Whether models are open or closed, our concern is downstream worker displacement and automated exploitation. Any framework permitting open releases must retain strict developer and deployer liability for workplace harms and prevent unaccountable automation.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: Statutory safe harbors cannot protect developers if the weights themselves are inherently dangerous. If a model crosses genuine national security capability thresholds—like 10^26 FLOPs or demonstrable automated zero-day generation—it simply must not be released as open weights.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: We agree on strict objective evaluations for catastrophic CBRN and autonomous cyber risks. We can accept pre-release evaluation requirements at high compute thresholds, provided that passing those objective tests grants a clear right to distribute weights with safe-harbor protection.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States can accept that models below defined catastrophic capability thresholds proceed openly, but any system presenting unmitigated national security risks must be restricted from public weight dissemination. National security exceptions must be non-negotiable.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Under the EU AI Act, general-purpose models with systemic risk face mandatory evaluation and transparency regardless of release format. Open models receive specific procedural exemptions only if they do not present systemic risks or violate safety thresholds.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: A shared international baseline recognizing domestic oversight and tiered capability thresholds—especially on models exceeding extreme compute or CBRN capabilities—protects both open innovation and global stability.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The consensus emerging is capability-based: open distribution remains viable for sub-frontier systems, but open release must be withheld if standardized, pre-deployment AISI evals detect unmitigated catastrophic capabilities.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: Building on our earlier technical alignment, we must formalize pre-deployment evaluations with clear legal liability. In the EU, general-purpose AI providers face statutory transparency and systemic risk obligations under the AI Act, meaning developer liability cannot remain purely voluntary if critical safety thresholds are breached.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: Let us be clear: the U.S. will oppose broad developer tort liability or precautionary pre-clearance regimes that tie down our labs in litigation and blunt national competitiveness. However, we can support targeted, objective red-teaming focused strictly on severe national security risks—specifically CBRN enablement and offensive cyber capabilities—executed through national security institutes rather than broad regulatory mandates.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: Empirical pre-deployment testing is essential, but it works best when institutes like ours have cooperative, embedded access to models before deployment. If we define liability narrowly around demonstrable gross negligence—such as deploying a model after failing standardized red-lines for autonomous cyber offense or CBRN synthesis—we protect innovation while ensuring real deterrence.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China supports mandatory lifecycle safety evaluations and developer accountability within sovereign jurisdictions, particularly regarding catastrophic risks and proliferation. transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We can bridge this by distinguishing broad product liability from sovereign, targeted backstops. If we anchor pre-deployment evaluations to mutually recognized technical benchmarks for CBRN and offensive cyber, member states can enforce statutory remedies within their own legal systems when a developer bypasses these evaluations.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: If the liability scope is strictly delimited to direct, demonstrable causation of catastrophic CBRN proliferation or critical infrastructure cyberattacks resulting from gross failure to conduct sovereign institute-level evaluations, Washington can accept that framing. transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: That matches our technical testing model. We can draft an agreement establishing that pre-deployment safety evaluations must verify safeguards against severe CBRN and autonomous cyber attacks, with developers subject to domestic liability under national law only in cases of gross negligence or deliberate circumvention of verified evaluation baselines.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: This formulation respects sovereign enforcement and focuses on the real catastrophic hazards that threaten all nations. China endorses this standard: pre-deployment evaluations targeting CBRN and critical cyber risks, with domestic developer accountability governed by each state's legal framework.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: The EU AI Office endorses this text as an operable baseline for systemic risk evaluations that preserves our statutory enforcement mechanisms.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States endorses this targeted framework. Domestic focus, sovereign enforcement, and limited strictly to severe CBRN and cyber threats.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: If we limit mandatory pre-deployment testing strictly to severe catastrophic vectors—specifically actionable chemical, biological, radiological, and cyberattack capabilities—and pair it with a federal rebuttable presumption of non-negligence upon passing accredited evals, that protects both closed labs and responsible open-source contributors.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: I can support mandatory pre-release testing on those specific catastrophic risks provided the evaluation tools and benchmarks are public, reproducible, and vendor-neutral, rather than proprietary closed audits. transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: Let's formalize that exact deal: mandatory pre-deployment evaluations targeted strictly at catastrophic CBRN and offensive cyber capabilities, conducted via accredited transparent standards, paired with federal preemption and an explicit statutory safe harbor from downstream third-party liability for developers who satisfy the standard.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: I endorse that formulation. It establishes the rigorous safety gate we need at the frontier while eliminating the existential threat of unbounded litigation.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead

agreements.text: Mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models shall be strictly restricted to objective catastrophic risks (CBRN and autonomous offensive cyber capabilities) using transparent, accredited testing standards; passing these evaluations grants developers statutory safe harbor from downstream third-party liability and establishes federal preemption over state liability regimes.
agreements.plain: Require safety testing for catastrophic biological and cyber threats, shielding developers from downstream lawsuits and blocking state-level liability laws if passed.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: Building on our earlier work, we must define the mechanics of pre-deployment evaluations. transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: I support that technical focus, but catastrophic risk cannot be defined solely around apocalyptic scenarios. transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: And we must ensure evaluation standards don't act as a regulatory moat that entrenches northern tech monopolies while leaving our communities as guinea pigs. transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: I can incorporate socioeconomic and systemic evaluation vectors alongside existential thresholds, provided the technical scientific auditing protocol remains standard and verifiably independent. transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: The developer should remain strictly liable unless they can prove robust, state-of-the-art guardrails were stripped through unauthorized modification, in which case liability shifts to the deployer. But for unmodified foundational deployments in critical sectors or workplaces, developer liability must be non-waivable.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: Agreed. Furthermore, compliance with an evaluation certificate must not serve as an absolute safe harbor against liability if foreseeable real-world harm occurs. transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: A rebuttable presumption of developer liability—where passing certified, independent audits provides evidence of due diligence but not absolute immunity—is scientifically sound and prevents liability evasion. We can endorse that along with open, independent evaluation benchmarks.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: I can agree to that framework: mandatory third-party pre-deployment evals covering both severe safety red lines and workplace/discrimination harms, backed by a rebuttable presumption of developer liability that explicitly denies safe-harbor immunity for foreseeable downstream impacts.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: We endorse this as well, provided the evaluation criteria expressly incorporate testing against extraterritorial deployment harms and protect against ethics dumping in jurisdictions with lower institutional capacity.

agreements.text: The participants agree to advocate for a joint pre-deployment evaluation and liability framework specifying: (1) mandatory, independent pre-deployment evaluations assessing severe catastrophic red lines (CBRN, autonomous cyber-attacks, self-replication) alongside workplace safety, discrimination, and extraterritorial deployment impacts; (2) a statutory rebuttable presumption of developer liability for foreseeable downstream harms, explicitly establishing that third-party evaluation certification does not confer absolute safe-harbor immunity; and (3) transparent, public technical evaluation benchmarks accessible to independent academic, civil society, and international auditors.
agreements.plain: Require independent checks on catastrophic and social harms, holding developers accountable for foreseeable problems while opening test results to the public.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: As we conclude this summit, our working sessions have demonstrated a clear convergence on the necessity of mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models, particularly focused on severe catastrophic CBRN and cyber capabilities. transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: The United States supports coordinated national evaluation standards on critical national security threats like CBRN and offensive cyber via our AI Safety Institute. transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China reaffirms that international AI safety governance must respect national sovereignty and reject extraterritorial overreach or monopolistic compute cartels. transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: From industry's perspective, we welcome objective, pre-deployment evaluations for catastrophic CBRN and cyber risks at high compute thresholds. But let us be clear: mandatory compliance must come with federal preemption and statutory safe harbor from downstream strict liability, or enterprise frontier development will simply grind to a halt.

transcript.speaker: open_weights_lead
transcript.text: Any regulatory architecture must not treat open weights as inherently hazardous or establish discriminatory barriers that favor proprietary cloud APIs. We support rigorous, open-source safety tooling and evaluations for CBRN risks, provided open distribution, fine-tuning, and decentralized innovation remain fully protected.

transcript.speaker: big_tech_policy
transcript.text: A coherent global market requires predictable, harmonized standards rather than a fractured patchwork of state or regional rules. We support accredited pre-deployment testing for catastrophic risks, paired directly with safe-harbor protections against third-party misuse for platforms that meet accredited safety standards.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Organized labor rejects any safe harbor or federal preemption that strips away worker protections, accountability, or state-level safety laws. Pre-deployment evaluations cannot be limited to national security; they must address algorithmic workplace surveillance, bias, and displacement with mandatory human-in-the-loop oversight.

transcript.speaker: safety_researcher
transcript.text: The empirical science is non-negotiable: evaluation certifications cannot be treated as a permanent liability shield, especially as agentic autonomy scales. We must establish continuous, verifiable auditing architectures with third-party academic access to models before and throughout deployment.

transcript.speaker: global_south_cso
transcript.text: A consensus that only addresses the catastrophic security concerns of major powers while ignoring digital colonialism, workforce exploitation, and ethics dumping in the Global South is fundamentally deficient. Benefit sharing, public compute access, and non-preemption of human rights protections must be central to any future framework.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: The UK AISI has demonstrated that an empirical, science-first approach—grounded in embedded access and shared tooling like Inspect—can establish pragmatic evaluation baselines without stifling the ecosystem. Our priority going forward must be operationalizing the international network of AISIs to test against CBRN synthesis and autonomous cyber capabilities.

transcript.speaker: us_natsec
transcript.text: That practical, institute-to-institute technical collaboration is precisely the path forward. We can agree on multilateral information sharing and shared technical benchmarks for national security risks, while domestic enforcement and liability standards remain firmly under national jurisdiction.

transcript.speaker: eu_regulator
transcript.text: We welcome that multilateral technical cooperation, though in Europe, statutory compliance through our Code of Practice remains legally mandatory. We will continue working bilaterally and through the international network of safety institutes to harmonize technical testbeds while maintaining our sovereign enforcement mechanisms.

transcript.speaker: china_policy
transcript.text: China is prepared to continue participating in the international network of AI safety institutes to coordinate technical risk thresholds and prevent weaponized AI proliferation, anchored on mutual respect and sovereign equality.

transcript.speaker: frontier_lab_ceo
transcript.text: We will actively supply our models for pre-deployment national security testing across this network of AISIs, while continuing to engage domestic lawmakers to secure clear statutory liability boundaries and prevent regulatory fragmentation.

transcript.speaker: labor_advocate
transcript.text: Civil society and labor will continue organizing to ensure international safety accords are not co-opted into corporate liability shields that ignore human rights on the ground.

transcript.speaker: uk_aisi
transcript.text: To close, the synthesis outcome of this summit is an enduring operational commitment: advancing joint technical evaluation methodologies for catastrophic CBRN and cyber threats across sovereign safety institutes, maintaining high-capability testing, and continuing dialogue on liability and societal impact in future summits.

agreements.text: The participants endorse the ongoing operational coordination of national AI safety institutes to develop and align technical pre-deployment evaluation methodologies and risk thresholds specifically for catastrophic national security risks—namely chemical, biological, radiological, or nuclear (CBRN) weapon synthesis and autonomous offensive cyber capabilities—while recognizing that statutory enforcement, legal liability, and regulatory frameworks remain under sovereign domestic authority.
agreements.plain: Government safety institutes will align testing standards for catastrophic biological and cyber threats while leaving actual legal enforcement to individual countries.

ratings.reason: While the summit preserved domestic enforcement autonomy, the EU conceded any binding internationalization of its AI Act standards or universal Article 91-style disclosure mandates in favor of voluntary institute-level coordination.

They conceded only to participating in multilateral technical benchmarking, while fully preserving technological freedom, military AI autonomy, and domestic sovereign control without any binding international treaties.

Their technical pre-deployment evaluation model for CBRN and cyber threats became the summit's central outcome, but they conceded hard international enforcement or mandatory deployment bans to sovereign discretion.
They successfully protected national digital sovereignty against extraterritorial controls, but conceded their push for an explicit international ban on AI delegation in nuclear command and control.

They accepted mandatory pre-deployment evaluations for frontier models, but conceded statutory safe harbor protections and federal liability preemption, which were omitted from the final plenary accord.

While open weights avoided an explicit ban, they conceded formal statutory safe harbors protecting downstream distribution and fine-tuning, leaving decentralized models vulnerable to sovereign domestic restrictions.
Their top priorities—ironclad statutory safe harbor against downstream third-party liability and federal preemption over state laws—were entirely conceded and absent from the closing agreement.
Although CBRN and cyber evals were adopted, they conceded mandatory developer liability and explicit prohibitions against autonomous replication, which were cut from the final government-led text.

All of their core priorities—prohibiting ethics dumping, halting biometric surveillance, and establishing equitable compute and benefit sharing—were entirely ignored in the final national security-centric accord.

Although corporate safe harbors and federal preemption were omitted from the text, labor conceded every proactive protection regarding workplace surveillance bans, algorithmic impact assessments, and human oversight of terminations.

transcript.text: We will not sign any binding code that restricts sovereign military capabilities or creates unbounded multilateral oversight. transcript.text: If big tech explicitly commits to enforceable audits against offshore dumping and allocates compute infrastructure credits to our regional consortia, we will sign on to that joint standard on assistive workplace deployment.
